strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: semantic segmentation without requiring users to supply an image-specific category vocabulary. Combining automatic vocabulary discovery with an existing segmentor offers practical value without additional model training.

BBoost provides a plausible technical contribution by decoding clustered subsets of BLIP features into local captions. Combining multiple clusterings and denoising their assignments is a sensible way to improve vocabulary coverage beyond global captioning.

Controlled experiments support the benefit of BBoost. With the same X-Decoder segmentor, Table 1 reports class-agnostic mIoU improvements from 38.0 to 71.8 on VOC and from 35.3 to 47.7 on PASCAL Context, with improvements on the other two datasets as well.

LAVE addresses a real evaluation difficulty involving synonyms and category granularity. Its scores are within 0.2–1.1 mIoU points of the manually constructed mappings across four datasets in Table 4, providing useful preliminary validation.

The diagrams, implementation settings, supplementary mapping pseudocode, and explicit failure cases help communicate the approach and its limitations. The main pretrained components and datasets are identified and cited.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol needs stronger validation. Section 9.3 relies on the LLM's recollection of the PASCAL Context and ADE20K vocabularies rather than supplying their actual class lists. Its prompts also direct stuff categories to background, which conflicts with scene-parsing annotations for terms not rescued by the exact-match override. Agreement in aggregate mIoU with manual mappings is encouraging, but does not establish mapping correctness or robustness to ambiguous and unmatched labels.

The comparison with ZeroSeg does not adequately separate vocabulary generation, segmentation backbone, and evaluation effects. The manuscript does not establish that ZeroSeg was evaluated using the same mapper and label-handling protocol. This matters because Table A7 shows that changing only the mapper shifts VOC performance by 9.6–13.2 points. Moreover, ZeroSeg already addresses segmentation without a supplied vocabulary, so the originality is primarily in BBoost and the proposed mapping approach rather than the task itself.

The separation between tuning and evaluation is unclear. Section 5.1 reports Bayesian optimization against VOC mIoU without identifying a disjoint tuning split, while the headline results select the best captioning-cycle count separately for each dataset from Table 2. Despite stochastic caption generation, repeated-run variability is not reported. These omissions weaken confidence in generalization and particularly in the small PASCAL Context improvement over ZeroSeg.

The evidence for accurate recognition beyond benchmark vocabularies remains mostly qualitative. Generating more distinct nouns does not establish that those labels correctly describe their assigned regions. Mapping predictions back to fixed categories also cannot verify finer distinctions within those categories. A systematic human audit of generated category-mask pairs, including incorrect and overly broad labels, would more directly support the central claims about semantic specificity and comprehensive scene understanding.

Several implementation and reporting ambiguities hinder reproduction. Equation 9 specifies independent maximum-IoU assignments despite the text describing Hungarian matching; alignment between the two spatial resolutions and handling of appended positional dimensions at the frozen decoder are insufficiently specified. Table A6 also claims one captioning cycle while reporting 87.1 VOC mIoU, whereas Table 2 reports 85.3 for one cycle and 87.1 for ten. These are potentially fixable issues, but the latter must be reconciled to interpret the denoising ablation reliably.
